items.title: Stop leaving pieces and mates unprotected
why: Hanging a piece, missing a free capture or walking into mate is 390 of your 1,019 big mistakes, and each one costs 27 to 45 win-% (a positional slip costs about 14).
Add the other missed tactics and tactical oversights and tactics are about 62% of everything that goes wrong.
do: Before every move ask three questions: what did their last move attack, is the square I'm moving to safe, and is anything of mine left undefended?
10 minutes a day of Lichess 'Hanging piece' and 'Mate in 1' puzzles until the check becomes automatic.

items.title: Slow down in the middlegame
why: You make 16.6 mistakes or blunders per 100 moves in the middlegame, against 6.9 in the opening and 9.2 in the endgame.
The middlegame holds 682 of your 1,019 big mistakes (352 mistakes and 330 blunders). The opening is not where you lose.
do: Spend your thinking time here, not in the first 8 moves. Play the opening moves from the repertoire quickly.
Each middlegame move: look for their checks, captures and threats first, then your plan.

items.title: Finish the games you are winning
why: You reached a clearly winning position (+3 or better) in 183 games and won only 95. That is 88 games thrown away.
56 of your 172 losses are on time. In 16 of those 56 you were ahead on the board when it happened, and 30 were already lost.
do: When ahead, trade pieces and avoid new risks. Do not hunt for extra material.
Practise the basic checkmates (two rooks, queen and king, king and rook) so you can finish fast.
Check your clock at move 20 and again at move 30. If you are ahead and low on time, play the simplest safe move.
items.measure: Win at least 75% of the games where you reach +3 (now 52%).

items.title: Play rapid for now, and cut blitz
why: Your blitz rating is about 313 and your rapid rating about 726.
31 of your 68 blitz losses (46%) are on time, against 25 of 104 rapid losses (24%). Low on the clock you make a big mistake on 16.4% of moves, against 11.8% otherwise.
do: Make 10-minute rapid your main practice format while the blunder check becomes a habit.
In blitz, play the opening from memory and save your clock for the middlegame.
items.measure: Timeout losses: 56 now. Aim for under 10% of your losses.

items.title: Learn the openings, in this order
why: Openings are the least costly problem, but three gaps are cheap to close: Black vs 1.d4 (9 wins, 23 losses), the Caro-Kann vs 2.Nf3 (7 wins, 15 losses) and the London vs the ...Bf5 mirror (0 wins, 3 losses).
do: 1. Learn the Slav setup against 1.d4 (2...c6, bishop out before ...e6).
2. Learn the Caro-Kann answers to 2.Nf3 and the Advance.
3. Keep the London as White. Try the Italian Game only after the first four priorities feel automatic.
items.measure: Review the 'Your openings' section once a week. Spend no more than 15 minutes a day on openings.

items.title: Review your biggest mistake after each loss
why: Your costliest blunders are shown on this page with the better move. Seeing the same patterns repeat is what builds the habit.
do: After a loss, find the one move where the game turned and say out loud what you missed.
Once a week, re-run this analysis and check the numbers above.
